headings.title: Clinical Indications and Purpose
headings.content: Vulva swabbing is a diagnostic procedure utilized primarily to identify infectious agents affecting the external female genitalia. Clinicians order this investigation when patients present with symptoms such as persistent vulvar pruritus, localized pain, abnormal discharge, or visible lesions like ulcers and vesicles. Common pathogens targeted during this sampling include **herpes simplex virus**, **candida species**, human papillomavirus, and bacterial agents responsible for sexually transmitted infections. Gathering accurate microbiological data ensures targeted antimicrobial therapy rather than empirical guessing, which helps combat resistance patterns increasingly observed in Nigerian healthcare settings.

headings.title: Anatomical Landmarks of the Vulva
headings.content:
A successful swab requires precise knowledge of external female anatomy to ensure the correct lesion or mucosal surface is sampled without causing unnecessary discomfort. 

- **Mons pubis**: The rounded fatty tissue overlying the pubic symphysis, covered with hair after puberty.
- **Labia majora**: The prominent, outer fleshy folds that protect the delicate structures medial to them.
- **Labia minora**: The thinner, hairless internal folds flanking the vaginal vestibule and urethral meatus.
- **Clitoris**: A highly sensitive erectile structure located at the anterior junction of the labia minora.
- **Bartholin's glands**: Located posteriorly at the 4 and 8 o'clock positions of the vaginal opening, frequent sites for painful duct cysts and abscesses.

headings.title: Equipment Preparation and Sterile Technique
headings.content: Gathering appropriate supplies beforehand prevents contamination and minimizes the time the patient spends in an uncomfortable position. Essential items include sterile examination gloves, a speculum if an internal inspection is simultaneously required, sterile transport swabs specific to the suspected pathogen, normal saline or sterile water to moisten dry swabs if necessary, and a proper waste disposal bin. Maintain strict **aseptic technique** throughout the setup by ensuring sterile packages remain unopened until the exact moment of use, preventing environmental bacteria from compromising the diagnostic sample.

headings.title: Patient Communication, Consent, and Positioning
headings.content: Intimate examinations can trigger significant anxiety and embarrassment for patients. Clear communication establishes psychological safety and builds therapeutic rapport. Explain every step of the procedure simply before touching the patient, and secure explicit verbal consent. Position the patient comfortably in the **dorsal lithotomy position**, ensuring proper draping to maintain privacy and dignity. Allow the patient to control the pace of the examination where clinically feasible, which fosters trust and reduces involuntary pelvic muscle guarding.

headings.title: Performing the Swab Procedure
headings.content: Execution requires gentle handling of inflamed or ulcerated tissues. Put on clean gloves, then gently separate the labia majora using your non-dominant hand to clearly visualize the target lesion, ulcer, or exudate. Take the sterile swab in your dominant hand. Rotate the swab firmly across the base of the lesion or active discharge site to capture sufficient cellular material and fluid, taking care not to touch surrounding healthy skin or the speculum edges. If testing for viral conditions like herpes, vigorously unroof a fresh vesicle to sample the fluid base where viral replication is highest. Place the tip directly into its designated transport vial immediately.

headings.title: Specimen Labeling, Handling, and Transport
headings.content: A perfectly collected sample is useless if mislabeled or degraded before reaching the laboratory. Immediately label the specimen container at the bedside in the presence of the patient, including full name, hospital number, date, time of collection, and anatomical site. Place the labeled vial into a biohazard specimen bag. Ensure prompt delivery to the microbiology laboratory; delays exceeding room temperature limits can cause fragile pathogens to die or overgrowth of commensal flora, resulting in unreliable diagnostic data.

headings.title: Infection Control and Safety Measures
headings.content: Standard precautions protect both the healthcare provider and subsequent patients from accidental transmission of bloodborne and sexually transmitted pathogens. Perform thorough hand hygiene before and after the procedure. Wear non-sterile gloves during physical contact with genital secretions, and change them if they touch any unintended non-sterile surface. Dispose of contaminated swabs and packaging in designated biohazard containers. Clean and disinfect reusable examination surfaces or speculums according to institutional protocols immediately after use.

headings.title: Documentation and Post-Procedure Care
headings.content: Careful closure of the encounter ensures continuity of care and legal accountability. Help the patient clean residual gel or discharge from the vulvar area using a soft tissue, and allow her to dress in privacy. Document the procedure thoroughly in the clinical notes, recording the date, time, specific indication, anatomical site swabbed, patient tolerance, and batch details of the transport kit. Inform the patient regarding expected result timelines and follow-up plans.
